The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is the deepest known point in the ocean, roughly 10,900 metres down.
Mount Everest would fit inside the Challenger Deep with about two kilometres of water to spare above its summit.
Water absorbs red light first. A few metres down, a red fish already looks dull; deeper, it can look almost black.
Below about 1,000 metres no sunlight reaches at all. The only light is made by animals.
Most deep-sea bioluminescence is blue, the colour that travels farthest through seawater.
Water pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every 10 metres of depth.
At the bottom of the Mariana Trench the pressure is more than 1,000 times that at the surface.
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first reached the Challenger Deep in the bathyscaphe Trieste on 23 January 1960.
Guam is the southernmost island of the Mariana archipelago.
Hydrothermal vents were first discovered in 1977, on the Galápagos Rift in the eastern Pacific.
Marine snow, a steady fall of organic particles from the sunlit ocean, feeds much of the life in the deep sea.
Coral reefs cover well under one percent of the seafloor, yet they are home to a large share of all known marine species.
The Mariana Trench Marine National Monument was established in 2009.
Sound travels about 1,500 metres per second in seawater, roughly four times faster than in air.
